name: ci-tls-smoke-warmup
title: Smoke test harness: build and warm up the TLS client context before connecting (fixes the intermittent Windows Debug TLS smoke failure)
issue: ROOT CAUSE (investigated, read-only, by an agent that read the harness, the host code and the logs of 11 passing and 2 failing Windows runs): the intermittent failure `SMOKE TEST FAILED: ConnectionAbortedError [WinError 10053]` with the host log `Closing an editor connection: its TLS handshake didn't finish within 5000 ms` in the job `windows (Debug, PhysX OFF, FreeType ON, ufbx ON, TLS ON)` step `Editor host TLS smoke test` is a TEST HARNESS problem, not a host bug: tests/smoke/n2_frames.py:101 connects first and only afterwards (lines ~110-114) builds the ssl.SSLContext and calls wrap_socket, so the Python process's FIRST TLS handshake (context construction, RNG seeding, algorithm fetches, key-share generation: on the runner's Python 3.12.10/OpenSSL 3.0 this costs 0.15 s to 8.6 s of CPU-bound work, round 1 always slow, round 2 7-14 ms) falls inside the host's 5 s handshake budget, which starts at accept. The host is behaving as designed (it times out a client that is silent for 5 s after connecting); a real editor client (Node tls.connect) prepares its TLS state before connecting. DO NOT raise the host's budget (that would only hide it). FIX (test harness only): in tests/smoke/n2_frames.py `connect` (and any other place in tests/smoke/*.py that connects to a TLS host): (1) build the SSLContext BEFORE socket.create_connection (once at module level or once per process, cached); (2) warm it up before connecting with an in-memory handshake: `ctx.wrap_bio(ssl.MemoryBIO(), ssl.MemoryBIO(), server_hostname=<the same server_hostname the real connection uses>).do_handshake()` inside try/except ssl.SSLWantReadError (this generates a ClientHello in memory, paying the first-use costs up front); make sure the warm-up cannot change the verification behaviour of the real connection (the real connection must still pin/verify the certificate fingerprint exactly as today: read the file to see how verification is done, and do not weaken it; the warm-up context may be a separate or the same context, but the warm-up object must be discarded); (3) print (to stdout) how long the real handshake took (ms) in the tls scenario, so future runs show the number; (4) keep Linux/macOS behaviour working and the tls and plain scenarios otherwise unchanged; (5) re-read the Python for syntax; if the file's line endings are CRLF/LF keep them. No engine/host change, no workflow change. Nothing can be run locally for this Windows-specific step: the PR's CI (10 checks, esp. the Windows Debug TLS leg and the Linux required leg) is the test: say that the flake is intermittent so a single green run is weak evidence; the proof is the printed handshake timings in the logs plus the absence of failures over the next runs. Add a short note to docs/testing.html only if an existing paragraph describes the TLS smoke test and would now be wrong.
acceptance: The TLS client context is built and warmed up before the TCP connect; certificate verification unchanged
The tls scenario prints the real handshake duration in ms
All 10 checks green; no host or workflow change
notes: Reviewer: certificate pinning/verification strictness unchanged (diff the verification code), warm-up uses no network and cannot throw uncaught, context created before connect, other smoke scenarios untouched, Python syntax and Windows paths.
